passages.happening:
“These are the names of the sons of Israel who went to Egypt with Jacob, each with his family” (verse 1). The names follow: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah and the rest (verses 2-4).

“The descendants of Jacob numbered seventy in all, including Joseph, who was already in Egypt” (verse 5).

“Now Joseph and all his brothers and all that generation died” (verse 6).

“but the Israelites were fruitful and increased rapidly; they multiplied and became exceedingly numerous, so that the land was filled with them” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Exodus begins in Hebrew with the word ‘and’. It does not start a new story. It carries on the one Genesis told. The list of Jacob's sons repeats Genesis 46 almost word for word, as if no book had ended. Before the story tells what Egypt did to this family, it reminds the reader who they are. They are a family with names.

The names are grouped by their mothers: Leah's sons first, then Rachel's Benjamin, then the sons of the two servant women. Joseph is missing from the list because he was already in Egypt.

Seventy is a small number, and that is the point. Verse 6 closes the book on Joseph's generation. They all die. Then verse 7 answers death with life. Listen to how many words it uses for growth: fruitful, increased, multiplied, exceedingly numerous, filled. Several of these are the words of God's blessing at creation, when he told the first humans to be fruitful and fill the earth. One of them, ‘increased rapidly’, is the Hebrew word for the swarming of fish and creatures in the waters on the fifth day. It is a startling word for a human family.

Some ancient copies count the family as seventy-five, not seventy. The Greek translation does, and so does one Hebrew copy of Exodus among the Dead Sea Scrolls. Stephen uses seventy-five in Acts 7:14. Both numbers were known in the first century. They count the family differently, and neither changes the story.

So the first readers hear two things at once. God's promise to Abraham of a great people is coming true. And it is coming true in a foreign land where this family has no rights at all.
passages.later:
The words of verse 7 come straight from creation: “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28). God said the same to Noah after the flood (Genesis 9:1), and he promised Abraham a family as many as the stars (Genesis 15:5).

Moses later reminds Israel how small they began: “Your fathers went down to Egypt, seventy in all, and now the LORD your God has made you as numerous as the stars in the sky” (Deuteronomy 10:22).

Stephen tells the same story in Acts: “As the time drew near for God to fulfill His promise to Abraham, our people in Egypt increased greatly in number” (Acts 7:17).
passages.asks: Exodus begins with a list of names before it tells a single event. Ask whether you believe God knows you by name, even when you feel like one small life in a long story. And ask where God may be keeping a promise in your life in a place that seems the wrong place for it.

passages.t: A king who did not know Joseph
passages.happening:
“Then a new king, who did not know Joseph, came to power in Egypt” (verse 8).

He says to his people, “the Israelites have become too numerous and too powerful for us. Come, let us deal shrewdly with them, or they will increase even more; and if a war breaks out, they may join our enemies, fight against us, and leave the country” (verses 9-10).

“So the Egyptians appointed taskmasters over the Israelites to oppress them with forced labor. As a result, they built Pithom and Rameses as store cities for Pharaoh” (verse 11).

“But the more they were oppressed, the more they multiplied and flourished; so the Egyptians came to dread the Israelites” (verse 12). “They worked the Israelites ruthlessly” (verse 13), and “made their lives bitter with hard labor in brick and mortar, and with all kinds of work in the fields” (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
With one sentence the story turns from blessing to threat. ‘A new king, who did not know Joseph’ may well have heard of Joseph. To ‘know’ in Hebrew means more than to be aware. It means to acknowledge and to honor. The new king refuses any duty to Joseph's memory or to Joseph's people. Forgetting is where the cruelty begins.

The chapter never names this king. ‘Pharaoh’ is a title, not a name. It comes from an Egyptian phrase meaning ‘great house’, first used of the royal palace and later of the king himself. Who this Pharaoh was depends on when the exodus happened, which is debated. Those who hold the early date look to the kings of the 1400s BC. Those who hold the later date think of Seti I or his son Ramesses II. The book page sets out both views.

Listen to the king's reasons. The Israelites are too many. They might join an enemy. They might leave. Every fear is ironic, because Israel will keep growing, and it will leave, not by joining an enemy but because God brings it out. ‘Come, let us deal shrewdly’ uses the Hebrew word for wisdom. It is wisdom bent to serve fear. And ‘Come, let us’ is how the builders of Babel spoke too (Genesis 11:4).

His first plan is forced labor under overseers. The Hebrew word for these work gangs, mas, is the same word later used of the crews King Solomon forced to work (1 Kings 5:13). Israel's own historians did not hide that their kings did it too.

Pithom and Rameses were store cities in the eastern Nile Delta, places to keep supplies. Rameses is usually identified with Pi-Ramesses, the great city of Ramesses II, which is one reason many favor the later date for the exodus; others think the name is an old place name brought up to date. Egypt built with sun-dried mud bricks. A painting in the tomb of Rekhmire, a high official in the 1400s BC, shows workers, some of them foreigners, making bricks under overseers.

The plan fails at once. The more they are crushed, the more they grow. Verses 13 and 14 are heavy on purpose. The Hebrew word for work or serve comes five times, and ‘ruthlessly’ opens and closes the two verses like a fence. ‘Made their lives bitter’ comes from the same root as the bitter herbs Israel would later eat at Passover.
passages.later:
God had told Abraham this would happen: “your descendants will be strangers in a land that is not their own, and they will be enslaved and mistreated four hundred years” (Genesis 15:13). And he had promised what would follow: “I will judge the nation they serve as slaves, and afterward they will depart with many possessions” (Genesis 15:14).

Israel's law took the rare Hebrew word behind ‘ruthlessly’ and forbade it among God's people: “You are not to rule over them harshly” (Leviticus 25:43). The BSB puts the same word as ‘harshly’ there. What was done to them in Egypt became what they must never do to one another.

Israel remembered these days at every harvest: “But the Egyptians mistreated us and afflicted us, putting us to hard labor” (Deuteronomy 26:6). And Stephen retells it: “Then another king, who knew nothing of Joseph, arose over Egypt” (Acts 7:18).
passages.asks: The king's cruelty began with fear of a people who were growing. Ask what you are afraid of losing, and whether that fear has ever made you hard toward others. Then ask what it would look like to remember, as Israel was told to remember, what it is to be on the weaker side.

passages.happening:
The king speaks to the Hebrew midwives, “whose names were Shiphrah and Puah” (verse 15). He orders them: “If the child is a son, kill him; but if it is a daughter, let her live” (verse 16).

“The midwives, however, feared God and did not do as the king of Egypt had instructed; they let the boys live” (verse 17).

The king summons them and asks, “Why have you let the boys live?” (verse 18). “The midwives answered Pharaoh, ‘The Hebrew women are not like the Egyptian women, for they are vigorous and give birth before a midwife arrives’” (verse 19).

“So God was good to the midwives, and the people multiplied and became even more numerous. And because the midwives feared God, He gave them families of their own” (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
The king's second plan is murder in secret. He gives the order himself, to two women.

Notice what the narrator does. The king of Egypt, the most powerful man in the world, is never named. The two midwives are. Their names are Shiphrah and Puah. The story tells you whose lives matter most in God's eyes.

Were they Hebrews or Egyptians? The Hebrew can be read either way: the Hebrew midwives, or the midwives of the Hebrew women. So no one can be sure. Later Jewish tradition said they were Moses' mother and sister, but the text does not say so.

The ‘birthstools’ were probably a pair of bricks or stones on which a woman knelt or crouched to give birth, as Egyptian women commonly did.

Then comes the first mention of God in the book of Exodus. He appears as the one the midwives fear. To fear God in the Old Testament is to take him more seriously than any human power. For two women with no rank at all, it meant defying the king. They did not do what the king ‘had instructed’. That phrase is used later in Exodus for obeying God. The midwives kept that kind of obedience for God alone.

Their answer to the king plays on a word. ‘Vigorous’ comes from the Hebrew word for life. The king asked why the boys lived. The midwives said, in effect, because their mothers are so full of life. The man who planned to ‘deal shrewdly’ is outwitted by two women he cannot check on.

God's answer is a gift that fits. The women who saved other women's families are given families of their own.
passages.later:
God's people would face this choice again. When the apostles were ordered to stop speaking of Jesus, they answered: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29). Daniel's three friends refused to bow to the king's statue (Daniel 3:16-18).

Rahab hid Israel's spies and misled the king's men who came for them (Joshua 2:4-6). Hebrews remembers her faith: “By faith the prostitute Rahab, because she welcomed the spies in peace, did not perish with those who were disobedient” (Hebrews 11:31).

And Proverbs says what the midwives knew: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom” (Proverbs 9:10).
passages.hard:
Did the midwives lie to Pharaoh, and did God reward a lie? The text does not say whether their answer was true, partly true, or a cover story. Most readers take it as a deception meant to protect the babies. What the text does say is why God was good to them: “because the midwives feared God” (verse 21). The reward is tied to their fear of God and their refusal to kill. It is not tied to their words.

Christians have weighed this in more than one way. Augustine held that lying is always wrong, and he argued that God rewarded the midwives' mercy, not their falsehood. Many others point to Rahab, and to people in every age who have hidden the innocent from those who wanted to kill them. They argue that misleading someone who is seeking to kill the innocent is not the false witness the commandment forbids, because the killer has no right to the truth he would use for murder.

Both views agree on what matters most. The midwives did right to refuse Pharaoh's order, and their courage is held up for honor. Faithful Christians differ on the question of their words, and these notes take no side.
passages.asks: Two women with no power said no to a king because they feared God more. Ask what pressures in your life compete with the fear of God. And ask whether there is a quiet act of courage God is asking of you, one that no one but God may ever see.

passages.happening: “Then Pharaoh commanded all his people: ‘Every son born to the Hebrews you must throw into the Nile, but every daughter you may allow to live’” (verse 22).
passages.hearers:
Labor did not work. Secret murder did not work. Now the king makes the killing of babies open policy, and he enlists his whole people in it. The chapter ends here, on this order, with nothing resolved.

The Nile was Egypt's life. Nearly all its people lived close to the river, and its yearly flood watered and fed the fields. Egyptians honored the flood as the god Hapi. Pharaoh turns the river of life into a river of death.

Remember this river. The next chapter opens with a Levite couple and a baby boy born under this order, and he will be drawn out of this very Nile. Later the first plague will turn the Nile to blood (7:20). And the army of the king who gave this order will perish in the sea (14:28). Exodus watches what Pharaoh does with water.

One small detail. The words ‘born to the Hebrews’ are not in the standard Hebrew text, which says only every son that is born. The BSB follows two ancient versions that add the words. Most translations supply them or something like them, since the meaning is clear from the story.

This verse is very dark. It is meant to be. The story does not hurry past the suffering of Israel's families. It names it, so that the rescue to come will be understood for what it is.
passages.later:
Stephen remembers it: “He exploited our people and oppressed our fathers, forcing them to abandon their infants so they would die” (Acts 7:19).

Matthew tells of another king who ordered boys killed. Herod “put to death all the boys in Bethlehem and its vicinity who were two years old and under” (Matthew 2:16), and the child Jesus escaped, as Moses would. Matthew does not quote Exodus here, but many readers see the pattern: God sends his deliverer into the very darkness where a tyrant kills children.

Hebrews honors the faith of the parents who defied this order: “By faith Moses’ parents hid him for three months after his birth, because they saw that he was a beautiful child, and they were unafraid of the king’s edict” (Hebrews 11:23).
passages.asks: The chapter ends in darkness, with God not yet named in the rescue. Ask what it means to you that Scripture does not hurry past suffering. And ask whether you can trust that God's silence, in a hard season, is not the same as his absence.
